highlights.text: ṣād-wāw-fāʾ is a single, sound root whose core meaning is الصُّوف (al-ṣūf), "wool"
A ram described as aṣwaf, ṣawif, ṣāʾif, or ṣāf is one that has abundant wool.
bukāʾ (with the long ending) = tears flowing from grief accompanied by wailing.
the pair points to gladness and sorrow as inner states
prevention / restraint — holding something back or blocking it.
Absala (أَبْسَلَ, Form IV) = "to give something up / surrender it to ruin."
Zuhayr's verse illustrates the sense: "If you two keep away from them, then they are basl [inaccessible/forbidden]."
one root with a single core sense: a shelter or dwelling
The noun is بَيْت (bayt, "house")
To plan or scheme a matter at night.
Hence the saying mā li-fulānin bītatu laylatin: "so-and-so hasn't even a night's provision (of food or the like) to get through the night on."
with a supporting line from the poet Umayya
this entry actually covers two distinct roots grouped together (d-f-ʾ, hamzated, and d-f-w/y, weak-final)
al-difʾ — the opposite of cold
"lakum fīhā difʾun wa manāfiʿ" — "for you in them [livestock] is warmth and [other] benefits."
al-dafaʾ as "a bending/stooping," applied in a hadith description of the Dajjāl
this root has a single underlying meaning: water, or a tear/weeping.
الدَّمْع (al-damʿ) = "the water of the eye," i.e. tears
O for an eye that never stops pouring forth — the tears have left a dimāʿ [tear-trace] upon it
a single root whose core sense is "what comes from fuel/kindling", i.e. smoke
al-dukhan is the ordinary word for smoke
The hadith phrase "hudnatun 'ala dakhan" ("a truce upon dakhan") - Ibn Faris glosses this as a settling or steadying upon matters that are disliked/detestable
as two distinct sound roots: (I) elevation/height, and (II) return/reversion
الفَوْق means loftiness.
Ibn Fāris glosses fawāq as: no returning, no relenting/repetition, no reversal.
Ibn Fāris cites al-Aʿshā: "until, when a fīqa had gathered in her udder, she came to suckle her heart's darling."
a hadith about the Qur'an: "atafawwaquhu tafawwuqa al-laqūḥ" — reading one's portion not all at once but in successive draughts
two sound roots: one meaning sufficiency, the other meaning a sound.
al-ghinā = wealth in property
al-ghanāʾ (with fatḥa and lengthening) = sufficiency.
al-ghunyān = wealth / self-sufficiency (cited from Qays).
to make oneself content or independent by means of something (i.e. to dispense with need of it). al-Aʿshā is cited
a single root whose core sense is strength and firmness/hardness.
جِلْد (jild) — "skin": well known, and stronger and firmer than the flesh beneath it.
said of a strong she-camel (with a verse: even when her spirit softens with fatigue, her bulk and strength remain)
a single core sense: the drawing-together or joining of a thing.
جَمَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ — "I gathered the thing."
to resolve or settle firmly on a course of action
A verse of Abū Qays contrasts a proper جَمْع (assembly) with a جُمَّاع (rabble).
with a verse of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza ("they resolved their affair by night…")
a single sound root meaning grasping and contracting
al-kaff is the human hand, named so because it grasps things.
mean "I held him back from the matter"
Ibn Muqbil speaks of "the surrounding (mustakiffa) eyes glancing".
one sound root whose core idea is mixing together and interpenetration.
لَبِسْتُ الثَّوْبَ ("I put on the garment") is the root meaning
We would have confused for them what they [already] make obscure
لِبَاس is used for a man's wife, and the husband is her libās — each clothes the other
the root's core sense as "the rising of a tongue of fire"
اللَّهَب (al-lahab) is the blaze/flame of a fire.
He quotes Imruʾ al-Qays' line pairing ulhūb (a shout-driven burst of speed) with dirra (leg-vigor) and a well-timed whip-strike that brings out a trained horse's best.
two sound (original) meanings: (1) being occupied and turned away from one thing by another, and (2) casting something from the hand.
al-lahw is anything that occupies you and diverts you from something else
al-Ḥasan and Qatāda glossed lahw here as "a woman/wife," while others glossed it as "a child/offspring."
a single sound root whose core sense is "a slight, non-prominent length"
لِسَان (lisān), "the tongue" — the familiar organ.
لِسْن (lisn) — a people's language: "every people has a lisn."
Shāhid: Ṭarafa, "when their tongues assail me, I am not a feeble, callow weakling."
joining one thing to another in an orderly, gathered arrangement
The verb naḍadtu means "I stacked/arranged [a thing] part upon part," either in neat order or one layer on top of another.
Illustrated by a line of al-Nābigha describing a stream let loose
the root's core sense of "drawing/extracting [water]."
istanbaṭa maʿnan ḥasanan / raʾyan ṣāʾiban — to deduce/draw forth a fine meaning or sound opinion
illustrated with a line of poetry by Kaʿb al-Ghanawī
One core meaning: elevation, strength, and prominence.
al-najd — an elevated road.
illustrated with a line of poetry by Ṭarafah about a glance at a woman striking the onlooker with an overwhelming affliction
one sound root whose core idea is prevention and holding back
النِّكْل, a fetter or shackle (plural أَنْكَال)
to do to a person something that prevents him from repeating the act and prevents others from doing the like
and hurl at the backs of their necks a mankal
the ḥadīth "God loves the nakal upon the nakal" is glossed within the report itself as the strong, experienced man on the strong, experienced horse
a sound root whose core meaning is "whiteness in a thing,"
al-qamar (the moon) is named for its whiteness
On al-Aʿshā's line taqammarahā ("an old man taqammara-ed her at night…")
a single, regular root whose core sense is springing/sending forth (inbiʿāth) and extension (imtidād)
al-mursalāt — the winds.
al-rasūl — the messenger; noted as well known, needing no gloss.
najda = hardship (with a supporting verse by Ṭarafa), and risl = ease/prosperity
here he states outright that the senses are too disparate — scarcely two of them share one pattern
He quotes Imru' al-Qays comparing two things to "the two water-skins of one in haste — freshly made, not yet greased with oil."
the root has one core meaning: pushing/repelling (al-dafʿ)
are named from this root because they push/drive (يَدْفَعُونَ) the people of Hell into it
A line of poetry is quoted praising a man for warding off blame with his wealth
a specific sale — selling fruit while it is still on top of the palm tree (unharvested) — which a ḥadīth forbids
one basic idea: inclining, swerving, turning aside from one direction toward another.
زُور (zūr) — falsehood. Named so because it leans away from the path of truth.
ازْوَرَّ عَنْ (izwarra ʿan) means to swerve away from something.
"They came with their two zūrs and we came with al-Aṣamm."
